claim: Gen1 expression is higher in proliferating pro-B, pre-B, and GC B cells than in follicular B, marginal zone B, and peritoneal B1a cells.
source: Expression of Gen1 is higher in the proliferating pro-B, pre-B, and GC B cells than in follicular B, marginal zone B, and peritoneal B1a cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data (GSE72018) shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mus81 RNA expression is relatively similar across all B cell subsets examined except in peritoneal B1a cells.
source: Conversely, Mus81 RNA expression is relatively similar across all B cell subsets examined except in peritoneal B1a cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data (GSE72018) shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Gen1 expression increases 10-fold as early as 24-hr post-activation in primary splenic naïve B lymphocytes stimulated with LPS and IL-4.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of primary splenic naïve B lymphocytes stimulated in culture with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and interleukin-4 (IL-4) revealed a 10-fold increase in Gen1 expression as early as 24-hr post-activation, while the expression of Mus81 was not altered following activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mus81 expression is not altered following activation of primary splenic naïve B lymphocytes with LPS and IL-4.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of primary splenic naïve B lymphocytes stimulated in culture with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and interleukin-4 (IL-4) revealed a 10-fold increase in Gen1 expression as early as 24-hr post-activation, while the expression of Mus81 was not altered following activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Gen1 expression is more closely associated with the activation and proliferation of B cells than is Mus81 expression.
source: We surmise that Gen1 expression is more closely associated with the activation and proliferation of B cells than is Mus81 expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential expression patterns of Gen1 and Mus81 upon B cell activation.

claim: Constitutive loss of both GEN1 and MUS81 leads to embryonic death.
source: Whereas Gen1−/− and Mus81−/− mice were born at the expected Mendelian frequencies, no live Gen1−/− Mus81−/− pups were produced, indicating that constitutive loss of both GEN1 and MUS81 leads to embryonic death (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by breeding data showing no live double knockout pups were produced, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The spleen cellularity of Mb1-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice is reduced by ninefold compared with control and single knockout mice.
source: We analyzed the spleen of the Mb1-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice and found that its cellularity was reduced by ninefold compared with that of control and single knockout mice (Figure 1C-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of spleen cellularity shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: Mb1-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice exhibit near complete ablation of mature B220+CD43+ and B220+CD43− cellular compartments.
source: The near complete ablation of mature B220+CD43+ and B220+CD43− cellular compartments indicated a significantly perturbed development or maintenance of peripheral B-lineage cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mb1-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice show a 75% reduction in total bone marrow cell number caused by severe loss of the total B cell population.
source: Examination of the BM revealed a 75% reduction in total cell number that was caused by the severe loss of the total B cell population; the T cell fraction remained unaltered (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of bone marrow cellularity and B cell populations shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Both immature and mature recirculating B cells are absent in the Mb1-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl bone marrows.
source: Quantification of the B-lineage subpopulations showed that both immature and mature recirculating B cells were absent in the Mb1-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl BMs (Figure 1H), and that the endonuclease-deficient B cell progenitors produced few CD19+ CD43+ CD249– CD24var pro-B cells (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of B cell subpopulations shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Endonuclease-deficient B cell progenitors in Mb1-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice produce few CD19+ CD43+ CD249– CD24var pro-B cells.
source: Quantification of the B-lineage subpopulations showed that both immature and mature recirculating B cells were absent in the Mb1-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl BMs (Figure 1H), and that the endonuclease-deficient B cell progenitors produced few CD19+ CD43+ CD249– CD24var pro-B cells (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of pro-B cells shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Gen1 and Mus81 in early B-cell precursors are necessary for the differentiation, expansion, or maintenance of developing pro-B cells.
source: These findings indicate that Gen1 and Mus81 in early B-cell precursors are necessary for the differentiation, expansion, or maintenance of developing pro-B cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the severe reduction in pro-B cells observed in Mb1-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice.

claim: The frequency and absolute number of GC B cells are decreased by 1.5- to 2-fold in DKO mice compared with control and SKO mice at steady-state.
source: We found that the frequency and absolute number of GC B cells were decreased by 1.5- to 2-fold in DKO mice compared with control and SKO mice (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of GC B cells in mesenteric lymph nodes and Peyer's patches shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Residual DKO GC B cells are attributed to the selection of GC B cells that have escaped Cre-mediated deletion of the Mus81fl/fl allele.
source: The presence of residual DKO GC B cells could be attributed to the selection of GC B cells that have escaped Cre-mediated deletion of the Mus81fl/fl allele, as evidenced by the detection of unrecombined Mus81fl/fl allelic copies and Mus81 mRNA transcript within the DKO GC B cell population compared with the near-complete deletion of Mus81fl/fl allele in the non-GC B cell counterpart (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic qPCR and RT-qPCR data showing unrecombined Mus81fl/fl allele and Mus81 mRNA in DKO GC B cells, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: GC formation is abrogated in DKO mice upon SRBC immunization, with GC frequency and absolute number being 5% of that observed in control and SKO mice.
source: Only in the DKO mice was GC formation abrogated: the frequency and absolute number of the GCs were 5% of that observed in control and SKO mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of GC B cells in SRBC-immunized mice shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The frequency of IgG1-switched cells is reduced by twofold in the sparse population of DKO GC B cells compared to control and SKO GCs after SRBC immunization.
source: Within the sparse population of DKO GC B cells that we could reliably detect, the frequency of IgG1-switched cells was reduced by twofold compared to that in control and SKO GCs; more importantly, the absolute count of these switched DKO cells was almost negligible (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of IgG1-switched GC B cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: The frequencies and absolute numbers of total B220+CD19+B cells in immunized DKO mice are comparable to their SKO and control littermates.
source: Despite the compromised GC response, the frequencies and absolute numbers of total B220+CD19+B cells in the immunized DKO mice were comparable to their SKO and control littermates (Figure 2F and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of total B cells in immunized mice shown in Figure 2F and H.

claim: Gen1-Mus81-null naïve B cells are unable to mount a productive GC reaction upon antigenic exposure at barrier sites and in secondary lymphoid organs.
source: These experiments indicate that although Gen1-Mus81-null naïve B cells can persist in the periphery, they are unable to mount a productive GC reaction upon antigenic exposure at the barrier sites and in secondary lymphoid organs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the abrogated GC response observed in DKO mice upon immunization.

claim: After 96 hr of culture, the number of live DKO cells is only 10% of that of control and SKO B cells across all stimulation conditions.
source: Across all stimulation conditions, the DKO B cells were unable to expand—after 96 hr of culture, the number of live DKO cells was only 10% of that of control and SKO B cells (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 72-hr post-stimulation, between 51% (LTD culture) and 68% (LPS culture) of DKO cells had undergone at least three rounds of cell division, compared to between 72% (LTD culture) and 86% (LPS culture) of control and SKO populations.
source: We noted that at 72-hr post-stimulation, between 51% (LTD culture) and 68% (LPS culture) of the DKO cells had underwent at least three rounds of cell division, in contrast to between 72% (LTD culture) and 86% (LPS culture) of the corresponding control and SKO populations (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by CellTrace Violet dilution analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The absolute numbers of division zero cells in DKO LI and LPS cultures are similar across all genotypes.
source: Although the DKO LI and LPS cultures contained a comparatively higher frequency of undivided (division zero) cells, the absolute numbers of division zero cells in both stimulations were similar across all genotypes, supporting the notion that the accumulation of division zero cells reflects a disproportionate representation of undivided DKO cells in the cultures caused by the progressive attrition of proliferating DKO cells, rather than by the specific inability of DKO cells to initiate cell division (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of division zero cells shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The lack of proliferative expansion of DKO B cells leads to minimal production of class-switched cells.
source: As cellular proliferation is intimately linked to class switching (Hodgkin et al., 1996; Rush et al., 2005), the lack of proliferative expansion of DKO B cells led to a minimal production of class-switched cells (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of class-switched cells shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, and by citations to prior work linking proliferation to class switching.

claim: As early as 48-hr post-stimulation, DKO cultures are enriched for cells in G2/M phase and depleted for cells in S phase.
source: As early as 48-hr post-stimulation, the DKO cultures were enriched for cells in G2/M phase and depleted for cells in S phase (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The skewed cell cycle distribution of DKO cells persists up till 96-hr post-activation and is observed in all culture conditions.
source: This skewed cell cycle distribution of the DKO cells persisted up till 96-hr post-activation and was observed in all culture conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: The concomitant loss of GEN1 and MUS81 causes cells to stall in G2/M, impeding the completion of the cell cycle.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the concomitant loss of GEN1 and MUS81 causes the cells to stall in G2/M, impeding the completion of the cell cycle.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cell cycle analysis showing G2/M enrichment in DKO cells.

claim: A 2- to 3-fold higher proportion of dead cells is observed in DKO cultures relative to control and SKO cultures.
source: Aside from the proliferation deficiency, we also observed a 2- to 3-fold higher proportion of dead cells in the DKO cultures relative to that in control and SKO cultures (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of dead cells shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: As early as 48-hr post-stimulation, the proportion of caspase-3+ cells is 2- to 5-fold higher in DKO cultures compared with control and SKO cultures.
source: As early as 48-hr post-stimulation, the proportion of caspase-3+ cells was 2- to 5-fold higher in DKO cultures compared with control and SKO cultures.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry analysis of cleaved caspase-3+ cells.

claim: The size of the caspase-3+ population peaks at 72-hr post-stimulation before declining (LI and LTD cultures) or remaining unchanged (LPS culture) at 96-hr post-stimulation.
source: The size of the caspase-3+ population peaked at 72-hr post-stimulation before declining (LI and LTD cultures) or remaining unchanged (LPS culture) at 96-hr post-stimulation (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of caspase-3+ cells over time shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Across all time points and stimulation conditions examined, DKO cells in G2/M and G0/G1 phases experience a 2- to 5-fold higher level of apoptosis than their control and SKO counterparts.
source: When we quantified the fraction of caspase 3+ cells in the different cell cycle phases, we found that across all the time points and stimulation conditions examined, DKO cells in G2/M and G0/G1 phases experienced a 2- to 5-fold higher level of apoptosis than their control and SKO counterparts (Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle-specific apoptosis analysis shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: GEN1 and MUS81 play an indispensable role in supporting the proliferative capacity and viability of activated B lymphocytes.
source: Taken together, these observations underscore an indispensable role for GEN1 and MUS81 in supporting the proliferative capacity and viability of activated B lymphocytes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the proliferation and survival defects observed in DKO B cells.

claim: Activated control and Gen1-KO B lymphocytes resemble each other transcriptomically.
source: The RNA-seq analysis showed that the activated control and Gen1-KO B lymphocytes resembled each other transcriptomically, consistent with the lack of overt perturbations in Gen1-KO B cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis comparing Mus81-KO to control cells identified 8 genes with a minimum of twofold upregulation in Mus81-KO cells.
source: Differential gene expression (DGE) analysis comparing Mus81-KO to control cells, however, identified 8 genes with a minimum of twofold upregulation in Mus81-KO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by DGE analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Between Gen1-KO and Mus81-KO cells, the transcript level of only four genes, including Mus81, are differentially altered.
source: Between Gen1-KO and Mus81-KO cells, the transcript level of only four genes, including Mus81, were differentially altered (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by DGE analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The deletion of either Gen1 or Mus81 alone does not substantially alter the transcriptional landscape of activated B lymphocytes.
source: These findings collectively illustrate that the deletion of either Gen1 or Mus81 alone does not substantially alter the transcriptional landscape of activated B lymphocytes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the minimal transcriptional changes observed in single knockout cells.

claim: 279 genes are upregulated by at least twofold (log2 fold change≥1; FDR<0.05) in DKO B cells compared to control cells.
source: DGE analysis of control versus DKO cells, on the contrary, revealed that 279 genes were upregulated by at least twofold (log2 fold change≥1; FDR<0.05) and 167 genes were downregulated by a minimum of log2 fold change of –0.3 in the DKO B cells (corresponding to a ≥19% de-enrichment relative to control cells) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by DGE analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 167 genes are downregulated by a minimum of log2 fold change of –0.3 in DKO B cells compared to control cells.
source: DGE analysis of control versus DKO cells, on the contrary, revealed that 279 genes were upregulated by at least twofold (log2 fold change≥1; FDR<0.05) and 167 genes were downregulated by a minimum of log2 fold change of –0.3 in the DKO B cells (corresponding to a ≥19% de-enrichment relative to control cells) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by DGE analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The p53 pathway is among the top five enriched gene sets in DKO cells, with 25/200 genes having log2 fold change≥1.
source: We identified the p53 pathway (25/200 genes with log2 fold change≥1; e.g., Ccng1, Zfp365, Plk2, Phlda3, Cdkn1a, and Zmat3) and apoptosis (15/161 genes with log2 fold change≥0.5) signatures among the top five enriched gene sets whereas gene sets containing targets of the transcription factors MYC and E2F and genes involved in progression through the G2/M checkpoint were among the most de-enriched in the DKO cells (Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-F), concurring with our findings that DKO cultures exhibit perturbed cell cycle progression, G2/M arrest, proliferation irregularities, and heightened apoptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Apoptosis signatures (15/161 genes with log2 fold change≥0.5) are among the top five enriched gene sets in DKO cells.
source: We identified the p53 pathway (25/200 genes with log2 fold change≥1; e.g., Ccng1, Zfp365, Plk2, Phlda3, Cdkn1a, and Zmat3) and apoptosis (15/161 genes with log2 fold change≥0.5) signatures among the top five enriched gene sets whereas gene sets containing targets of the transcription factors MYC and E2F and genes involved in progression through the G2/M checkpoint were among the most de-enriched in the DKO cells (Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-F), concurring with our findings that DKO cultures exhibit perturbed cell cycle progression, G2/M arrest, proliferation irregularities, and heightened apoptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Gene sets containing targets of the transcription factors MYC and E2F and genes involved in progression through the G2/M checkpoint are among the most de-enriched in DKO cells.
source: We identified the p53 pathway (25/200 genes with log2 fold change≥1; e.g., Ccng1, Zfp365, Plk2, Phlda3, Cdkn1a, and Zmat3) and apoptosis (15/161 genes with log2 fold change≥0.5) signatures among the top five enriched gene sets whereas gene sets containing targets of the transcription factors MYC and E2F and genes involved in progression through the G2/M checkpoint were among the most de-enriched in the DKO cells (Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-F), concurring with our findings that DKO cultures exhibit perturbed cell cycle progression, G2/M arrest, proliferation irregularities, and heightened apoptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Ex vivo-activated DKO B cells display a robust type I IFN gene signature, with high enrichment score (NES=2.35; FDR=6.34×10–3) and induction (log2 fold change≥0.5) of 21/97 genes in the gene set.
source: We also noted that the ex vivo-activated DKO B cells displayed a robust type I IFN gene signature, as exemplified by the high enrichment score (NES=2.35; FDR=6.34×10–3) and the induction (log2 fold change≥0.5) of 21/97 genes in the gene set (e.g., Ifit3, Ifit3b, Ifitm3, Mx1, and Rsad2) (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The deficiency of both GEN1 and MUS81 in cells activates p53-dependent pathways to arrest cell cycle for the repair of genomic insults sustained during cellular growth and proliferation, and to initiate apoptosis when such DNA lesions are beyond tolerance and repair.
source: We posit from this analysis that the deficiency of both GEN1 and MUS81 in cells activates p53-dependent pathways to arrest cell cycle for the repair of genomic insults sustained during cellular growth and proliferation, and to initiate apoptosis when such DNA lesions are beyond tolerance and repair.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the transcriptional signatures observed in DKO cells.

claim: The deletion of p53 does not restore the abrogated GC response of DKO B cells.
source: Our genetic study showed that the loss of p53 was insufficient to rescue the abrogated GC response and proliferative expansion of DKO B cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of DKO Trp53-KO mice.

claim: The deletion of p53 does not restore the proliferative expansion of DKO B cells.
source: Our genetic study showed that the loss of p53 was insufficient to rescue the abrogated GC response and proliferative expansion of DKO B cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of DKO Trp53-KO mice.

claim: p53 deletion prevents apoptosis of ex vivo-activated DKO B cells early on, but this survival benefit is only temporary.
source: Though p53 deletion did prevent apoptosis of ex vivo-activated DKO B cells early on, this survival benefit was only temporary as the p53-null DKO B cells experienced much higher level of cell death at later time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by apoptosis analysis of DKO Trp53-KO cells over time.

claim: p53-null DKO B cells experience much higher level of cell death at later time points.
source: Though p53 deletion did prevent apoptosis of ex vivo-activated DKO B cells early on, this survival benefit was only temporary as the p53-null DKO B cells experienced much higher level of cell death at later time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by apoptosis analysis of DKO Trp53-KO cells over time.

claim: The absence of p53 precludes DKO p53-KO cells from arresting their cell cycle despite incurring extensive replication-associated DNA damage, leading to mitotic catastrophe and their eventual demise.
source: We infer that the absence of p53 precludes the DKO p53-KO cells from arresting their cell cycle despite incurring extensive replication-associated DNA damage, leading to mitotic catastrophe and their eventual demise.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that p53 deletion does not rescue DKO cells and they experience increased cell death at later time points.

claim: DKO B cells display approximately six times as many chromosomal abnormalities per metaphase as control and SKO B cells.
source: DKO B cells displayed approximately six times as many abnormalities per metaphase as control and SKOs B cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of chromosomal aberrations in metaphase spreads shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Almost 95% of control and SKO metaphases have no more than two aberrations.
source: Furthermore, whereas almost 95% of control and SKO metaphases had no more than two aberrations, 45% of DKO metaphases showed three or more chromosomal defects (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of chromosomal aberrations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 45% of DKO metaphases show three or more chromosomal defects.
source: Furthermore, whereas almost 95% of control and SKO metaphases had no more than two aberrations, 45% of DKO metaphases showed three or more chromosomal defects (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of chromosomal aberrations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Chromosomal aberrations, including breaks, DNA fragments, fusions, and radials, are detected at an elevated rate in DKO B cells compared with control and SKO cells.
source: Chromosomal aberrations, including breaks, DNA fragments, fusions, and radials, were detected at an elevated rate in DKO B cells compared with control and SKOs cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of specific types of chromosomal aberrations shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 67% of the breaks observed in DKO cells are chromosome-type breaks that occur at the same position on both sister chromatids.
source: Notably, 67% of the breaks observed were chromosome-type breaks that occur at the same position on both sister chromatids (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of break types shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In DKO cells, chromosomal breakage occurs proximal to the telomeres, resulting in paired DNA fragments containing telomeric DNA.
source: In DKO cells, the breakage occurred proximal to the telomeres, resulting in paired DNA fragments containing telomeric DNA (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Tel-FISH analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Symmetrical breakage proximal to telomeres has been proposed to arise from unresolved recombination intermediates.
source: Such symmetrical breakage has been proposed to arise from unresolved recombination intermediates (Garner et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Garner et al., 2013.

claim: The absence of GEN1 and MUS81 engenders an assortment of chromosomal lesions in proliferating B cells.
source: These observations show that the absence of GEN1 and MUS81 engenders an assortment of chromosomal lesions in proliferating B cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the diverse chromosomal aberrations observed in DKO B cells.

claim: Ablation of AID does not restore the proliferative and survival capacities of DKO cells.
source: Ex vivo culture studies showed that the deletion of AID did not restore the proliferative and survival capacities of DKO cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of DKO Aicda-KO cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: The average number of chromosomal aberrations in DKO Aicda-KO cells is similar to that of DKO Aicda-Het B cells.
source: Additionally, the average number of chromosomal aberrations in the DKO Aicda-KO cells was similar to that of DKO Aicda-Het B cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of chromosomal aberrations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E.

claim: AID-driven DSBs contribute little to the severe proliferation and viability defects exhibited by Gen1-Mus81-null B lymphocytes.
source: These findings illustrate that AID-driven DSBs contribute little to the severe proliferation and viability defects exhibited by Gen1-Mus81-null B lymphocytes and that the chromosomal aberrations occurring within the DKO B cells are likely caused by unrepaired replication-associated DNA damage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AID deletion does not rescue DKO cell defects.

claim: The chromosomal aberrations occurring within DKO B cells are likely caused by unrepaired replication-associated DNA damage.
source: These findings illustrate that AID-driven DSBs contribute little to the severe proliferation and viability defects exhibited by Gen1-Mus81-null B lymphocytes and that the chromosomal aberrations occurring within the DKO B cells are likely caused by unrepaired replication-associated DNA damage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AID deletion does not rescue DKO cell defects.

claim: Inactivation of both GEN1 and MUS81 in early B cell precursors abolishes the production of mature B cells in the BM and periphery.
source: Inactivation of both enzymes in early B cell precursors abolished the production of mature B cells in the BM and periphery, whereas ablation in mature, naïve B cells impaired GC formation in response to antigenic stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of Mb1-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice.

claim: Ablation of GEN1 and MUS81 in mature, naïve B cells impairs GC formation in response to antigenic stimulation.
source: Inactivation of both enzymes in early B cell precursors abolished the production of mature B cells in the BM and periphery, whereas ablation in mature, naïve B cells impaired GC formation in response to antigenic stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of Cd23-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice.

claim: Endonuclease-deficient B cells exhibit significant proliferation and viability perturbations underpinned by widespread chromosomal abnormalities and activation of cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in response to protracted p53 signaling elicited by extensive DNA damage.
source: Ex vivo cellular and transcriptomics analyses revealed that these endonuclease-deficient B cells exhibited significant proliferation and viability perturbations underpinned by widespread chromosomal abnormalities and activation of cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in response to protracted p53 signaling elicited by extensive DNA damage.
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo culture studies, RNA-seq analysis, and metaphase spread analysis of DKO B cells.

claim: The severe attrition of pro-B cells in Mb1-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice could be caused by a developmental arrest during the transition from pre-pro B cell to pro-B cell stage, by proliferation and survival defects of the pro-B cells, or both.
source: The severe attrition of pro-B cells in the Mb1-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice could be caused by a developmental arrest during the transition from pre-pro B cell to pro-B cell stage, by proliferation and survival defects of the pro-B cells, or both.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the possible causes of pro-B cell loss.

claim: Pro-B cells undergo IL-7R-dependent proliferative expansion prior to V(D)J recombination.
source: Pro-B cells, compared to the mitotically inactive pre-pro B cells, undergo IL-7R-dependent proliferative expansion prior to V(D)J recombination and so are more likely to suffer from intense replication stress that could necessitate commensurate effort of replication restart (Hardy et al., 1991; Peschon et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Hardy et al., 1991 and Peschon et al., 1994.

claim: SSE-knockout pro-B cells are unable to resolve both stalled replication forks and recombination-associated DNA structures formed during restart activities, leading to failure to thrive and proliferate.
source: As the SSE-knockout pro-B cells are unable to resolve both stalled replication forks and recombination-associated DNA structures formed during such restart activities, they would fail to thrive and proliferate further.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the known functions of GEN1 and MUS81 and the observed phenotype of SSE-knockout pro-B cells.

claim: The lack of robust chronic and induced GC responses in Cd23-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice can be ascribed to the inability of DKO cells to alleviate replication stress generated during sustained proliferation by eliminating replication-induced junction molecules, leading to G2/M stalling and abrogation of a complete cell division.
source: Similarly, the lack of robust chronic and induced GC responses in the Cd23-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice can be ascribed to the inability of DKO cells to alleviate replication stress generated during sustained proliferation by eliminating replication-induced junction molecules, leading to G2/M stalling and abrogation of a complete cell division.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed GC defects and cell cycle perturbations in DKO cells.

claim: High levels of concurrent DNA replication and transcriptional activities within GC B cells could promote replication-transcription conflicts and R-loop formation that further exacerbate replication stress.
source: High levels of concurrent DNA replication and transcriptional activities within the GC B cells could promote replication-transcription conflicts and R-loop formation that further exacerbate replication stress.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about replication-transcription conflicts and R-loop formation.

claim: Arrested DKO cells could not tolerate for long periods the high level of DNA damage incurred from multiple rounds of cell division and consequently undergo mitotic catastrophe.
source: We did not observe a time-dependent G2/M accumulation in the DKO culture, suggesting that the arrested DKO cells could not tolerate for long periods the high level of DNA damage incurred from multiple rounds of cell division and consequently undergo mitotic catastrophe, evidenced in the comparatively higher rate of apoptosis among cells in the G2/M phase.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of time-dependent G2/M accumulation and the high apoptosis rate in G2/M phase cells.

claim: Resting mature DKO cells persist unscathed in the spleen, as exemplified by the normal frequencies and numbers of splenic B cell subpopulations in Cd23-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice.
source: Resting mature DKO cells, however, persisted unscathed in the spleen, as exemplified by the normal frequencies and numbers of splenic B cell subpopulations in the Cd23-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of splenic B cell populations in Cd23-Cre Gen1−/− Mus81fl/fl mice.

claim: Splenic naïve B cells do not self-renew; instead, they are constantly replenished from immature precursors produced in the BM and maintained homeostatically by the survival signals BAFF and APRIL.
source: Splenic naïve B cells do not self-renew; instead, they are constantly replenished from immature precursors produced in the BM and maintained homeostatically by the survival signals BAFF and APRIL (Hao and Rajewsky, 2001; Mackay and Gommerman, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Hao and Rajewsky, 2001 and Mackay and Gommerman, 2015.

claim: Resting mature B cells are spared from replication-derived genotoxicity, rendering GEN1 and MUS81 dispensable in these cells.
source: Hence, resting mature B cells are spared from replication-derived genotoxicity, rendering GEN1 and MUS81 dispensable in these cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that resting mature DKO B cells persist normally in the spleen.

claim: The inability of the BTR complex to compensate for the concomitant deficiencies of GEN1 and MUS81 suggests that DNA replication and recombination events generate persistent double HJs and multiple BTR-refractory HJ species such as single HJs and nicked HJs that must be resolved by these endonucleases.
source: The inability of the BTR complex to compensate for the concomitant deficiencies of GEN1 and MUS81 and maintain the viability of proliferating DKO B cells suggests that DNA replication and recombination events generate persistent double HJs and multiple BTR-refractory HJ species such as single HJs and nicked HJs that must be resolved by these endonucleases to suppress genomic instability and catastrophic mitosis (García-Luis and Machín, 2014).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the severe phenotype of DKO cells and supported by citation to García-Luis and Machín, 2014.

claim: The MUS81-EME2 complex mediates replication fork restart by endonucleolytic cleavage of stalled replication forks during S phase to protect genome integrity.
source: In particular, the MUS81-EME2 complex has been shown to mediate replication fork restart by endonucleolytic cleavage of stalled replication forks during S phase to protect genome integrity (Pepe and West, 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Pepe and West, 2014a.

claim: When MUS81 is unavailable, GEN1 can potentially act on replication intermediates (or a processed form of them) that persist into mitosis upon nuclear breakdown to initiate HR-dependent fork restart.
source: Although the in vivo relevance of GEN1 in processing such intermediates remains to be formally established, our genetic analysis and others suggest that when MUS81 is unavailable, GEN1 can potentially act on these substrates (or a processed form of them) that persist into mitosis upon nuclear breakdown to initiate HR-dependent fork restart (García-Luis and Machín, 2014; Ho et al., 2010; Sarbajna et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by the genetic analysis in this study and citations to prior work by García-Luis and Machín, 2014; Ho et al., 2010; and Sarbajna et al., 2014.

claim: Deficiency in SSEs enables the uncleaved D-loop to undergo prolonged extension, promoting mutagenesis, template switching, and nonreciprocal loss of heterozygosity.
source: Deficiency in these SSEs enables the uncleaved D-loop to undergo prolonged extension, promoting mutagenesis, template switching, and nonreciprocal loss of heterozygosity (Ho et al., 2010; Mayle et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Ho et al., 2010 and Mayle et al., 2015.

claim: SSEs can act on nascent D-loops to promote the less deleterious genetic outcome of half crossovers and on extended D-loops to restrict error-prone DNA synthesis.
source: SSEs can presumably act on nascent D-loops to promote the less deleterious genetic outcome of half crossovers and on extended D-loops to restrict error-prone DNA synthesis (Mayle et al., 2015; Schwartz and Heyer, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Mayle et al., 2015 and Schwartz and Heyer, 2011.

claim: The observation of extensive chromosomal aberrations in endonuclease-null mouse B cells concurs with that of Sarbajna et al., 2014 that employed siRNA depletion of Gen1 and Mus81 in cells treated with replication inhibitors.
source: Our observation of extensive chromosomal aberrations in the endonuclease-null mouse B cells concur with that of Sarbajna et al., 2014 that employed siRNA depletion of Gen1 and Mus81 in cells treated with replication inhibitors.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to prior work by Sarbajna et al., 2014.

claim: Recombination intermediates generated in S phase that fail to be resolved in the absence of GEN1 and MUS81 evade the checkpoint response and persist into mitosis, generating homologous recombination ultrafine bridges (HR-UFBs).
source: Recombination intermediates generated in S phase that fail to be resolved in the absence of GEN1 and MUS81 evade the checkpoint response and persist into mitosis, generating homologous recombination ultrafine bridges (HR-UFBs) (Chan et al., 2018; Mohebi et al., 2015; Tiwari et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Chan et al., 2018; Mohebi et al., 2015; and Tiwari et al., 2018.

claim: Breakage of HR-UFBs during cytokinesis engenders chromosomal breaks that activate the DNA damage checkpoint in the next cell cycle, triggering non-homologous end joining-mediated fusion of DNA ends that leads to widespread chromosomal rearrangements.
source: Breakage of the HR-UFBs during cytokinesis engenders chromosomal breaks that activate the DNA damage checkpoint in the next cell cycle, triggering non-homologous end joining-mediated fusion of DNA ends that leads to widespread chromosomal rearrangements (Chan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Chan et al., 2018.

claim: The preponderance of chromosome breaks that appear to occur at identical sites on sister chromatids suggests that the aberrations result from defective resolution of inter-chromatid recombination intermediates.
source: The preponderance of chromosome breaks that appear to occur at identical sites on sister chromatids suggest that the aberrations result from defective resolution of inter-chromatid recombination intermediates (Kikuchi et al., 2013; Shimizu et al., 2020; Wechsler et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of chromosome-type breaks and supported by citations to prior work by Kikuchi et al., 2013; Shimizu et al., 2020; and Wechsler et al., 2011.

claim: Unresolved HJs have been implicated to impede DNA condensation in mitosis, manifesting as 'pinches' in the chromosome.
source: Unresolved HJs have been implicated to impede DNA condensation in mitosis, manifesting as 'pinches' in the chromosome (Wechsler et al., 2011); thus, a subset of the chromosome breaks observed in DKO cells may not be actual breaks but rather intact HJs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Wechsler et al., 2011.

claim: A subset of the chromosome breaks observed in DKO cells may not be actual breaks but rather intact HJs.
source: Unresolved HJs have been implicated to impede DNA condensation in mitosis, manifesting as 'pinches' in the chromosome (Wechsler et al., 2011); thus, a subset of the chromosome breaks observed in DKO cells may not be actual breaks but rather intact HJs.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the known behavior of unresolved HJs.

claim: MUS81—and potentially GEN1—cleaves stalled replication forks to initiate BIR and MiDAS at CFS and other under-replicated regions.
source: We also cannot completely exclude the role of MUS81—and potentially GEN1—in cleaving stalled replication forks to initiate BIR and MiDAS at CFS and other under-replicated regions where such failure leads to the formation of FANCD2-flanking fragile site-UFBs (FS-UFBs) between the segregating chromatids (Naim et al., 2013; Ying et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citations to prior work by Naim et al., 2013 and Ying et al., 2013.

claim: The frequent occurrence of breaks at corresponding locations on paired sister chromatids argues for a failure of DKO B cells to resolve HR intermediates.
source: However, the frequent occurrence of breaks at corresponding locations on paired sister chromatids argues for a failure of DKO B cells to resolve HR intermediates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of chromosome-type breaks.

claim: The study presents the first evidence that the ablation of both GEN1 and MUS81 induces the expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs).
source: Our study presents the first evidence that the ablation of both GEN1 and MUS81 induces the expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs), most likely attributed to the elevated levels of micronuclei in the DKO cells (Sarbajna et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing ISG expression in DKO cells and inferred to be attributed to micronuclei based on citation to Sarbajna et al., 2014.

claim: Primary human fibroblast cells lacking the BLM dissolvase exhibit an enhanced ISG gene expression signature due to the increased level of cytoplasmic DNA and cGAS-positive micronuclei.
source: Primary human fibroblast cells lacking the BLM dissolvase exhibit an enhanced ISG gene expression signature due to the increased level of cytoplasmic DNA and cGAS-positive micronuclei in these cells, suggesting a common transcriptional outcome in cells that fail to eliminate recombination-associated structures (Gratia et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Gratia et al., 2019.

claim: Micronuclei are formed when chromosomal fragments or lagging chromosomes—manifestations of mitotic or DNA repair defects—become enveloped in a rupture-prone nuclear membrane after failing to be incorporated into the nucleus after mitosis.
source: Micronuclei are formed when chromosomal fragments or lagging chromosomes—manifestations of mitotic or DNA repair defects—become enveloped in a rupture-prone nuclear membrane after failing to be incorporated into the nucleus after mitosis (Miller et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Miller et al., 2021.

claim: Recognition of micronuclei by cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS) triggers the catalytic production of the second messenger cyclic 2′3′-GMP-AMP (2′3′-cGAMP), promoting the phosphorylation of the adaptor stimulator of interferon genes (STING) that mediates the activation of interferon-regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) to drive the transcription of ISGs.
source: Recognition of the micronuclei by cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS) triggers the catalytic production of the second messenger cyclic 2′3′-GMP-AMP (2′3′-cGAMP), promoting the phosphorylation of the adaptor stimulator of interferon genes (STING) that mediates the activation of interferon-regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) to drive the transcription of ISGs (Harding et al., 2017; Li and Chen, 2018; Mackenzie et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Harding et al., 2017; Li and Chen, 2018; and Mackenzie et al., 2017.

claim: Production and release of chromatin fragments from spontaneously ruptured micronuclei and from improper degradation of nascent DNA at unprotected, stalled replication forks further contribute to the cytosolic pool of immunostimulatory DNA fragments.
source: Production and release of chromatin fragments from spontaneously ruptured micronuclei and from improper degradation of nascent DNA at unprotected, stalled replication forks further contribute to the cytosolic pool of immunostimulatory DNA fragments (Coquel et al., 2018; Dou et al., 2017; Emam et al., 2022; Glück et al., 2017; Ragu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Coquel et al., 2018; Dou et al., 2017; Emam et al., 2022; Glück et al., 2017; and Ragu et al., 2020.

claim: DNA-stimulated type I IFN signaling triggers various cell death programs including apoptosis, necroptosis, and autophagic cell death.
source: DNA-stimulated type I IFN signaling, besides promoting the synthesis and secretion of proinflammatory cytokines, triggers various cell death programs including apoptosis, necroptosis, and autophagic cell death (Paludan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Paludan et al., 2019.

claim: p53 signaling can be directly activated by STING via cyclic dinucleotides to trigger cell cycle arrest and apoptosis independent of type I IFN production.
source: Recent evidence in T cells, however, suggests that p53 signaling can be directly activated by STING via cyclic dinucleotides to trigger cell cycle arrest and apoptosis independent of type I IFN production (Concepcion et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Concepcion et al., 2022.

claim: The cytoplasm of DKO B cells could accumulate a panoply of self-DNA materials that fosters the production of 2′3-cGAMP and type I IFNs, initiating multiple cell death pathways simultaneously.
source: We speculate that the cytoplasm of the DKO B cells could accumulate a panoply of self-DNA materials that fosters the production of 2′3-cGAMP and type I IFNs, initiating multiple cell death pathways simultaneously.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed ISG expression and known mechanisms of cGAS-STING signaling.

claim: Macrophages and T cells can import 2′3′-cGAMP via the heteromeric anion channels LRRC8A-LRRC8E and LRRC8A-LRRC8C, respectively, to activate STING and type I IFN production.
source: This raises the question as to whether the cGAS-STING cascade comprises a secondary cell death signaling axis in the SSE-null cells, and whether micronucleated DKO B cells could elicit cell death in neighboring cells through the paracrine release of 2′3′-cGAMP and type I IFNs, given that macrophages and T cells can import 2′3′-cGAMP via the heteromeric anion channels LRRC8A-LRRC8E and LRRC8A-LRRC8C, respectively, to activate STING and type I IFN production (Concepcion et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Concepcion et al., 2022 and Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: The illegitimate processing of branched DNA structures and the persistence of unresolved HR intermediates generated following replication fork stalling and recombination-mediated fork restart in proliferating B cells lacking GEN1 and MUS81 lead to the manifestation of aberrant mitotic structures including chromatin bridges, HR-UFBs, and micronuclei.
source: We posit that the illegitimate processing of branched DNA structures and the persistence of unresolved HR intermediates generated following replication fork stalling and recombination-mediated fork restart in proliferating B cells lacking GEN1 and MUS81 lead to the manifestation of aberrant mitotic structures including chromatin bridges, HR-UFBs, and micronuclei that enable rampant fusions of broken chromosomes and amplification of replication-derived DNA damage during the next cell cycle.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed chromosomal aberrations and known functions of GEN1 and MUS81.

claim: Extensive chromosomal instability and genomic damage in DKO B cells activate p53-dependent G2/M arrest and apoptosis.
source: Our studies show that such extensive chromosomal instability and genomic damage consequently activate p53-dependent G2/M arrest and apoptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observed cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and p53 transcriptional signature in DKO cells.

claim: Endonuclease-deficient B cells exhibit a type I IFN transcriptional signature, potentially a ramification of high levels of cytoplasmic self-DNA.
source: Concurrently, these endonuclease-deficient B cells exhibit a type I IFN transcriptional signature, potentially a ramification of high levels of cytoplasmic self-DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing ISG expression and inferred to be caused by cytoplasmic self-DNA.

claim: The synthetic lethality of GEN1 and MUS81 deficiencies in B cells highlights the essentiality of SSEs in eliminating branched and joint DNA intermediates formed during replication, recombination, and repair events to safeguard the genomic integrity of proliferating cells.
source: The synthetic lethality of GEN1 and MUS81 deficiencies in B cells highlights the essentiality of SSEs in eliminating branched and joint DNA intermediates formed during replication, recombination, and repair events to safeguard the genomic integrity of proliferating cells and to confer the proliferative and survival capacities required for the proper development and functionality of B lymphocytes, and possibly other immune cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the severe phenotypes observed in DKO B cells.
